title: Find Lucky Integer in an Array
notes:
Task and constraints: Return the largest integer whose frequency in the array equals the integer itself, or -1 if none exists.
Idea: Count each integer's frequency and select the largest value whose count equals the value itself; default to `-1` when none qualifies.
Technique and why it applies: Frequency equality defines a lucky value, and taking the maximum among matches gives the required largest one.
Invariant: The frequency map records exact occurrences, and `best` is the greatest qualifying value encountered.
Edge cases: A value with zero or mismatched frequency is not lucky; return -1 if no candidate qualifies.
Complexity: O(n) time and O(u) space for u distinct values.
complexity_reason: Frequency equality defines a lucky value, and taking the maximum among matches gives the required largest one.

title: Find Lucky Integer in an Array
notes:
Task and constraints: Return the largest integer whose frequency in the array equals the integer itself, or -1 if none exists.
Idea: Count each integer's frequency and select the largest value whose count equals the value itself; default to `-1` when none qualifies.
Technique and why it applies: Frequency equality defines a lucky value, and taking the maximum among matches gives the required largest one.
Invariant: The frequency map records exact occurrences, and `best` is the greatest qualifying value encountered.
Edge cases: A value with zero or mismatched frequency is not lucky; return -1 if no candidate qualifies.
Complexity: O(n) time and O(u) space for u distinct values.
code:
import java.util.*;
class Solution { public int findLucky(int[] arr){Map<Integer,Integer>c=new HashMap<>();for(int x:arr)c.put(x,c.getOrDefault(x,0)+1);int ans=-1;for(Map.Entry<Integer,Integer>e:c.entrySet())if(e.getKey().equals(e.getValue()))ans=Math.max(ans,e.getKey());return ans;} }
complexity_reason: Frequency equality defines a lucky value, and taking the maximum among matches gives the required largest one.

title: Minimum Subsequence in Non-Increasing Order
approach_name: Take largest values until majority sum
notes:
Task and constraints: Return the shortest subsequence, sorted non-increasingly, whose sum is greater than the sum of the remaining elements.
Idea: Sort values descending and append the largest values until the selected sum exceeds the sum of all remaining values.
Technique and why it applies: Taking values from largest downward reaches a strict majority with the fewest elements.
Invariant: The selected sum grows with each largest value; stopping at the first strict majority yields the shortest qualifying subsequence.
Edge cases: The inequality must be strict; all values are positive under the problem constraints; output order is non-increasing.
Complexity: O(n log n) time and O(n) space for sorting/output.
complexity_reason: Taking values from largest downward reaches a strict majority with the fewest elements.

title: Minimum Subsequence in Non-Increasing Order
approach_name: Take largest values until majority sum
notes:
Task and constraints: Return the shortest subsequence, sorted non-increasingly, whose sum is greater than the sum of the remaining elements.
Idea: Sort values descending and append the largest values until the selected sum exceeds the sum of all remaining values.
Technique and why it applies: Taking values from largest downward reaches a strict majority with the fewest elements.
Invariant: The selected sum grows with each largest value; stopping at the first strict majority yields the shortest qualifying subsequence.
Edge cases: The inequality must be strict; all values are positive under the problem constraints; output order is non-increasing.
Complexity: O(n log n) time and O(n) space for sorting/output.
code:
import java.util.*;
class Solution { public List<Integer> minSubsequence(int[] nums){Arrays.sort(nums);List<Integer>out=new ArrayList<>();int total=0;for(int x:nums)total+=x;int cur=0;for(int i=nums.length-1;i>=0;i--){out.add(nums[i]);cur+=nums[i];if(cur>total-cur)break;}return out;} }
complexity_reason: Taking values from largest downward reaches a strict majority with the fewest elements.

title: Kids With the Greatest Number of Candies
notes:
Task and constraints: For each child, return whether giving them extraCandies would make their candy count at least the current maximum.
Idea: Find the current maximum candy count and return for each child whether `candies[i]+extraCandies` is at least that maximum.
Technique and why it applies: Comparing each boosted count to the original maximum answers every child's hypothetical eligibility.
Invariant: The maximum is fixed from the original array, and each boolean independently tests the child's hypothetical count against it.
Edge cases: Equality qualifies; children are assessed independently; empty arrays are excluded by the problem constraints.
Complexity: O(n) time and O(n) output space.
complexity_reason: Comparing each boosted count to the original maximum answers every child's hypothetical eligibility.

title: Kids With the Greatest Number of Candies

Technique and why it applies: Comparing each boosted count to the original maximum answers every child's hypothetical eligibility.
Invariant: The maximum is fixed from the original array, and each boolean independently tests the child's hypothetical count against it.
Edge cases: Equality qualifies; children are assessed independently; empty arrays are excluded by the problem constraints.
Complexity: O(n) time and O(n) output space.
code:
import java.util.*;
class Solution { public List<Boolean> kidsWithCandies(int[] candies,int extraCandies){int m=0;for(int x:candies)m=Math.max(m,x);List<Boolean>out=new ArrayList<>();for(int x:candies)out.add(x+extraCandies>=m);return out;} }
complexity_reason: Comparing each boosted count to the original maximum answers every child's hypothetical eligibility.

title: Destination City
approach_name: Find city never appearing as an origin
notes:
Task and constraints: Given directed city paths that form one non-cyclic route, return the destination city with no outgoing path.
Idea: Collect every path origin into a set, then return the destination from the route that never appears among origins.
Technique and why it applies: The final city is exactly the destination label that never occurs as a path origin.
Invariant: A city in the route with no outgoing edge is absent from the origin set.
Edge cases: The paths form one non-cyclic route under the statement; there is one terminal destination.
Complexity: O(n) time and O(n) space.
complexity_reason: The final city is exactly the destination label that never occurs as a path origin.

Technique and why it applies: The final city is exactly the destination label that never occurs as a path origin.
Invariant: A city in the route with no outgoing edge is absent from the origin set.
Edge cases: The paths form one non-cyclic route under the statement; there is one terminal destination.
Complexity: O(n) time and O(n) space.
code:
import java.util.*;
class Solution { public String destCity(List<List<String>> paths){Set<String>s=new HashSet<>();for(List<String>p:paths)s.add(p.get(0));for(List<String>p:paths)if(!s.contains(p.get(1)))return p.get(1);return ""; }
complexity_reason: The final city is exactly the destination label that never occurs as a path origin.

title: Build an Array With Stack Operations
approach_name: Simulate reading values from 1 through n
notes:
Task and constraints: Return Push and Pop operations to build target from the stream 1..n, stopping when target is complete.
Idea: Read integers from 1 through `n`, append `Push` for each read value, append `Pop` when the value is not the next target element, and stop once target is built.
Technique and why it applies: Simulating the input stream emits exactly the push/pop operations needed to retain target values.
Invariant: The simulated stack contains the target prefix after each accepted value; discarded stream values are removed immediately.
Edge cases: Stop as soon as all target values are produced; target values are increasing and drawn from the stream.
Complexity: O(n) time in the largest scanned stream prefix and O(n) operation-list space.
complexity_reason: Simulating the input stream emits exactly the push/pop operations needed to retain target values.

title: Build an Array With Stack Operations
approach_name: Simulate reading values from 1 through n
notes:
Task and constraints: Return Push and Pop operations to build target from the stream 1..n, stopping when target is complete.
Idea: Read integers from 1 through `n`, append `Push` for each read value, append `Pop` when the value is not the next target element, and stop once target is built.
Technique and why it applies: Simulating the input stream emits exactly the push/pop operations needed to retain target values.
Invariant: The simulated stack contains the target prefix after each accepted value; discarded stream values are removed immediately.
Edge cases: Stop as soon as all target values are produced; target values are increasing and drawn from the stream.
Complexity: O(n) time in the largest scanned stream prefix and O(n) operation-list space.
code:
import java.util.*;
class Solution { public List<String> buildArray(int[] target,int n){Set<Integer>w=new HashSet<>();for(int x:target)w.add(x);List<String>out=new ArrayList<>();for(int x=1;x<=target[target.length-1];x++){out.add("Push");if(!w.contains(x))out.add("Pop");}return out;} }
complexity_reason: Simulating the input stream emits exactly the push/pop operations needed to retain target values.

title: Number of Students Doing Homework at a Given Time
notes:
Task and constraints: Count students whose startTime <= queryTime <= endTime.
Idea: Count intervals satisfying `startTime[i] <= queryTime <= endTime[i]`.
Technique and why it applies: The inclusive interval predicate directly models whether each student is active at the requested time.
Invariant: The running count includes precisely the student intervals that cover the query instant.
Edge cases: Both interval endpoints are inclusive; a student finishing or starting exactly at queryTime counts.
Complexity: O(n) time and O(1) auxiliary space.
code:
class Solution:
 def busyStudent(self,startTime,endTime,queryTime):return sum(a<=queryTime<=b for a,b in zip(startTime,endTime))
complexity_reason: The inclusive interval predicate directly models whether each student is active at the requested time.

title: Number of Students Doing Homework at a Given Time
notes:
Task and constraints: Count students whose startTime <= queryTime <= endTime.
Idea: Count intervals satisfying `startTime[i] <= queryTime <= endTime[i]`.
Technique and why it applies: The inclusive interval predicate directly models whether each student is active at the requested time.
Invariant: The running count includes precisely the student intervals that cover the query instant.
Edge cases: Both interval endpoints are inclusive; a student finishing or starting exactly at queryTime counts.
Complexity: O(n) time and O(1) auxiliary space.
code: class Solution { public int busyStudent(int[] startTime,int[] endTime,int queryTime){int ans=0;for(int i=0;i<startTime.length;i++)if(startTime[i]<=queryTime&&queryTime<=endTime[i])ans++;return ans;} }
complexity_reason: The inclusive interval predicate directly models whether each student is active at the requested time.

title: Make Two Arrays Equal by Reversing Subarrays
notes:
Task and constraints: Return true if two arrays can be made equal using reversals of any subarrays.
Idea: Compare element frequency maps (or sorted copies) for the two arrays; arbitrary subarray reversals can realize any permutation, so matching multisets are sufficient.
Technique and why it applies: Subarray reversals can reorder elements arbitrarily, making multiset equality the necessary and sufficient condition.
Invariant: The frequency difference for every value is zero exactly when the arrays contain the same multiset.
Edge cases: Order may differ; duplicate counts must match; equal lengths are guaranteed by the problem.
Complexity: O(n) expected time and O(n) space for frequency maps, or O(n log n) if sorting copies.
complexity_reason: Subarray reversals can reorder elements arbitrarily, making multiset equality the necessary and sufficient condition.

import java.util.*;
class Solution { public boolean canBeEqual(int[] target,int[] arr){int[]a=target.clone(),b=arr.clone();Arrays.sort(a);Arrays.sort(b);return Arrays.equals(a,b);} }
complexity_reason: Subarray reversals can reorder elements arbitrarily, making multiset equality the necessary and sufficient condition.

title: Shuffle the Array
notes:
Task and constraints: Transform [x1,...,xn,y1,...,yn] into [x1,y1,...,xn,yn].
Idea: For each index `i` in the first half, append `nums[i]` followed by `nums[i+n]` to interleave the two halves.
Technique and why it applies: Indexing corresponding positions in the two halves constructs the alternating output directly.
Invariant: After each iteration, the output contains the first i pairs in the requested x/y order.
Edge cases: The input has exactly two halves of length n; preserve each pair's original order.
Complexity: O(n) time and O(n) output space.
complexity_reason: Indexing corresponding positions in the two halves constructs the alternating output directly.

title: Shuffle the Array
notes:
Task and constraints: Transform [x1,...,xn,y1,...,yn] into [x1,y1,...,xn,yn].
Idea: For each index `i` in the first half, append `nums[i]` followed by `nums[i+n]` to interleave the two halves.
Technique and why it applies: Indexing corresponding positions in the two halves constructs the alternating output directly.
Invariant: After each iteration, the output contains the first i pairs in the requested x/y order.
Edge cases: The input has exactly two halves of length n; preserve each pair's original order.
Complexity: O(n) time and O(n) output space.
code: class Solution { public int[] shuffle(int[] nums,int n){int[]out=new int[nums.length];for(int i=0;i<n;i++){out[2*i]=nums[i];out[2*i+1]=nums[i+n];}return out;} }
complexity_reason: Indexing corresponding positions in the two halves constructs the alternating output directly.

title: Final Prices With a Special Discount in a Shop
notes:
Task and constraints: For each price, subtract the first subsequent price that is less than or equal to it, if one exists.
Idea: Maintain a monotonic stack of unresolved price indices; when the current price is no greater than the price at the top, apply it as that earlier item's first eligible discount.
Technique and why it applies: The monotonic stack resolves each price at the first later value that is no greater than it.
Invariant: Indices remaining on the stack have not yet encountered a later price less than or equal to their own.
Edge cases: Equal prices qualify as discounts; items without a qualifying later price keep their original value.
Complexity: O(n) time because each index is pushed and popped once, and O(n) stack/output space.
complexity_reason: The monotonic stack resolves each price at the first later value that is no greater than it.

title: Final Prices With a Special Discount in a Shop
notes:
Task and constraints: For each price, subtract the first subsequent price that is less than or equal to it, if one exists.
Idea: Maintain a monotonic stack of unresolved price indices; when the current price is no greater than the price at the top, apply it as that earlier item's first eligible discount.
Technique and why it applies: The monotonic stack resolves each price at the first later value that is no greater than it.
Invariant: Indices remaining on the stack have not yet encountered a later price less than or equal to their own.
Edge cases: Equal prices qualify as discounts; items without a qualifying later price keep their original value.
Complexity: O(n) time because each index is pushed and popped once, and O(n) stack/output space.
code: class Solution { public int[] finalPrices(int[] prices){int[]out=prices.clone();ArrayDeque<Integer>st=new ArrayDeque<>();for(int i=0;i<prices.length;i++){while(!st.isEmpty()&&prices[st.peek()]>=prices[i])out[st.pop()]-=prices[i];st.push(i);}return out;} }
complexity_reason: The monotonic stack resolves each price at the first later value that is no greater than it.

title: Running Sum of 1d Array
notes:
Task and constraints: Return the running sum where output[i] is the sum of nums[0..i].
Idea: Maintain a cumulative total, add each input value, and write the current total to the corresponding output position.
Technique and why it applies: A single running accumulator computes every prefix sum without rescanning earlier elements.
Invariant: After processing index i, the total equals the sum of `nums[0..i]`.
Edge cases: Negative values are included normally; empty input produces an empty output.
Complexity: O(n) time and O(n) output space.
complexity_reason: A single running accumulator computes every prefix sum without rescanning earlier elements.

title: Running Sum of 1d Array
notes:
Task and constraints: Return the running sum where output[i] is the sum of nums[0..i].
Idea: Maintain a cumulative total, add each input value, and write the current total to the corresponding output position.
Technique and why it applies: A single running accumulator computes every prefix sum without rescanning earlier elements.
Invariant: After processing index i, the total equals the sum of `nums[0..i]`.
Edge cases: Negative values are included normally; empty input produces an empty output.
Complexity: O(n) time and O(n) output space.
code: class Solution { public int[] runningSum(int[] nums){int[]out=new int[nums.length];int sum=0;for(int i=0;i<nums.length;i++){sum+=nums[i];out[i]=sum;}return out;} }
complexity_reason: A single running accumulator computes every prefix sum without rescanning earlier elements.
